modules.title: Personal experiences and change
modules.summary: Narrate past events clearly, separate finished past from life experience, and describe habits that changed over time.
modules.lightGrammar: used to / would; present perfect continuous

grammar.name: Narrative tenses
grammar.explanation: When you tell a story, past continuous sets the scene, past simple moves the action forward, and past perfect explains what had already happened.
keyPoints: Past continuous frames the background: I was walking home when I saw the message.
Past perfect marks the earlier of two past events: the film had already started.
Keep one main timeline; use past perfect only when the order matters.
grammar.example: I had been waiting for hours when the bus finally arrived, so I walked the last two kilometres.

items.prompt: When I arrived, the film ___.
items.explanation: Past perfect shows the film started before you arrived.

items.prompt: I ___ home when I saw the message.
items.explanation: Past continuous sets the background action interrupted by a shorter event.

items.prompt: We ___ for hours before the bus finally came.
items.explanation: Past perfect continuous emphasises duration before a later past moment.

grammar.name: used to / would; present perfect continuous
grammar.explanation: Use used to (or would for repeated past actions) for past habits that have stopped, and present perfect continuous for an activity that started in the past and is still continuing or just stopped with visible results.
keyPoints: Used to works for both past states (I used to live in Leeds) and repeated actions.
Would is only for repeated past actions, never stative verbs like live, be, or know.
Present perfect continuous highlights duration up to now: I have been commuting by bike for six months.
grammar.example: I used to drive to work every day, but I have been cycling since April and feel much fitter.

items.prompt: Before moving to Bristol, I ___ live in a tiny flat near the harbour.
items.explanation: "Live" is a state, so use "used to" rather than "would".

items.prompt: She ___ English for three years and still takes two classes a week.
items.explanation: Present perfect continuous connects an ongoing activity from the past into the present.

items.prompt: Every summer, our family ___ walk along the coastal path before breakfast.
items.explanation: "Would" describes repeated past actions in a nostalgic narrative.

vocab.definition: gradually change your behaviour or habits to deal with a new situation
vocab.example: It took me a few months to adapt to life in Manchester.
vocab.note: Followed by to, then a noun or -ing form.

gapFill.prompt: It took my sister several months to ___ living in a much larger city.
gapFill.explanation: Use "adapt to" followed by a noun or an -ing verb form.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a time you had to adapt to a new routine, city, or job.

vocab.definition: the moment at which a situation changes in an important or decisive way
vocab.example: Moving to Leeds was a turning point for me.
collocations: a turning point in my life

gapFill.prompt: Switching careers at thirty turned out to be a major ___ in my life.
gapFill.explanation: "A turning point" is a countable noun phrase meaning a decisive moment of change.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Describe a turning point in your education, career, or personal life.

vocab.definition: something new and difficult that tests your ability or determination
vocab.example: She faced a real challenge in her first year at university.

gapFill.prompt: Although the new role looked daunting, Dan was eager to ___ the challenge.
gapFill.explanation: Common B2 collocations are "face a challenge" and "rise to the challenge".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write one sentence about a real challenge you faced and how you handled it.

vocab.definition: become comfortable and familiar with a new home, school, or job
vocab.example: The children settled in quickly at their new school.
vocab.note: Not followed by an object (UK/US natural everyday phrasal verb).

gapFill.prompt: Everyone in the team was friendly, which helped me ___ during my first week.
gapFill.explanation: "Settle in" is intransitive (no object) and means to feel at home in a new place.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about how long it took you to settle in somewhere new.

vocab.definition: gradually develop from a child into an adult
vocab.example: I grew up in a small town near Bristol.
collocations: grow up in a small town

gapFill.prompt: My grandparents ___ in a coastal village before moving inland for work.
gapFill.explanation: "Grow up" takes no object; parents "bring up" children, while children "grow up".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence comparing where you grew up with where you live today.

vocab.definition: think about something that happened in your past
vocab.example: When I look back on that year, I realise how much I changed.

gapFill.prompt: When I ___ my student days in Cardiff, I realise how much I learnt.
gapFill.explanation: "Look back on" must be followed by a noun phrase object (e.g. "those years").

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence starting with "When I look back on..." about an important year.

vocab.definition: feel sorry or disappointed about something you did or did not do
vocab.example: I don't regret leaving my job. I have no regrets.
vocab.note: Regret + -ing for the past (UK/US: identical pattern).

gapFill.prompt: She never regretted ___ her flat in London to move closer to the sea.
gapFill.explanation: Use "regret + -ing" when talking about a past decision you feel sorry (or not sorry) about.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence using "regret + -ing" or "have no regrets" about a past choice.

vocab.definition: slowly, over a long period of time rather than all at once
vocab.example: My English improved gradually over the winter.

gapFill.prompt: At first she felt nervous speaking aloud, but her confidence ___ grew over the term.
gapFill.explanation: "Gradually" means little by little over time, the opposite of "suddenly".

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence about a skill or habit that changed gradually for you.

vocab.definition: worth remembering or easy to remember because it was special
vocab.example: Our first night in Edinburgh was truly memorable.
vocab.note: Positive; often used with experience, trip, day.

gapFill.prompt: Hearing live folk music in an old pub made our weekend in Galway truly ___.
gapFill.explanation: "Memorable" is an adjective with a positive meaning, often paired with experience, trip, or night.

vocab.sentencePrompt: Write a sentence describing a memorable trip, day, or conversation.

inputs.title: Three people, three changes
inputs.body: LAURA: I had been teaching for six years when I finally booked a one-way ticket. I was terrified, but it turned out to be the best decision I have ever made. DIEGO: My parents came round to the idea eventually. At first they thought I was throwing away a good job, and to be honest, so did I. MARI: I only really settled down at thirty-five. Before that I was moving every eighteen months, and I had never owned furniture that I actually chose myself. Later in the programme, all three guests reflected on how difficult the very first month felt. Priya admitted she had nearly packed her bags after two weeks of grey skies, yet staying through that winter gave her a steady confidence she still relies on today. Dan noted that switching from long-haul flights to local rail journeys saved him time as well as money, while Rosa realised that teaching neighbours in person kept her grounded whenever work grew hectic.

questions.prompt: How long had Laura been teaching before she booked the ticket?
How do Diego's parents feel now?
What does Mari say about her earlier life?

inputs.title: The year everything changed
inputs.body: Most people can name the year their life changed. For Ana it was 2020, when the restaurant she managed closed for good. She had spent a decade building a career she loved, and suddenly it had gone. What she remembers now is not the loss but the noise of it: one week she was planning a menu, the next she was queuing for a job she had never imagined doing. Two years later she runs a small cooking school, and she says she would not go back. The turning point, she insists, was not the closure itself but the first morning she stopped waiting for things to return to normal. At first, the slower pace felt uncomfortable because she had spent five years measuring every evening in completed tasks. Gradually, however, she noticed that walking to the corner shop without checking her phone made her far more observant. She started speaking to the baker, trading recipes with an elderly neighbour, and reading novels she had kept on her shelf for years. By December, the move no longer felt like an interruption to her career; instead, it had become the turning point that showed her what kind of daily rhythm she genuinely wanted to keep.

questions.prompt: What does she remember most clearly?
What does Ana identify as her real turning point?

speaking.title: A turning point in your life (60–90s)

writing.title: Informal email: news and changes
writing.prompt: Write an informal email to a friend you have not contacted for a year. Tell them about one change in your life, ask two questions, and suggest meeting. 120–150 words.

outline.analyze: Purpose: share news and re-connect. Audience: a friend. Register: informal but correct.
outline.plan: Greeting → one clear change → two questions → suggestion → sign-off.
outline.draft: Use present perfect for news, past simple for finished details, and at least two phrasal verbs.
outline.improve: Replace 'very good' and 'nice' with precise adjectives; add one linker per paragraph.
outline.review: Check the word count, the greeting and closing, and that both questions are clear.

collocations.example: Leaving my hometown was a big decision to make at twenty-two.
collocations.note: Always use "make" (never "do") with "decision".

collocations.example: They took a risk by opening a bakery during a quiet winter.
collocations.note: Fixed collocation: "take a risk", not "make a risk".

collocations.example: It took me several months to get used to living alone after university.
collocations.note: "Get used to" is followed by a noun or -ing form (here, "living").

collocations.phrase: keep in touch with old friends
collocations.example: Even after moving to Glasgow, I tried to keep in touch with old friends.
collocations.note: Opposite: "lose touch with someone".

collocations.example: Once I started speaking for ten minutes a day, I began to make real progress.
collocations.note: Uncountable: "make progress" (never "a progress").

collocations.example: She took up a new hobby — pottery — to unwind after busy shifts.
collocations.note: Phrasal verb "take up" means start a sport, hobby, or regular activity.

modules.title: Plans, goals and ambitions
modules.summary: Distinguish arrangements, fixed intentions, and spontaneous decisions, and review zero, first, and second conditionals.

grammar.name: Future forms: plans, predictions, arrangements
grammar.explanation: Choose the future form by meaning: going to for intentions, will for predictions and spontaneous decisions, present continuous for fixed arrangements.
keyPoints: Fixed arrangement: I'm meeting my manager at nine tomorrow.
Intention: I'm going to apply for the internal role.
Prediction or offer: It will probably take two years. I'll send it now.
grammar.example: I'm meeting the recruiter on Thursday, and I'm going to take the online course before then; it will make the interview easier.

items.prompt: I ___ the recruiter at nine tomorrow — it is already in my calendar.
items.explanation: A fixed arrangement takes the present continuous.

items.prompt: Which sentence expresses an intention?
options: I'm going to retrain next year.
items.answer: I'm going to retrain next year.
items.explanation: 'Going to' expresses a plan or intention rather than a promise.

items.prompt: The job ___ harder than it looks.
items.explanation: Predictions about the future use will + infinitive.

grammar.name: Conditionals 0–2 (review)
grammar.explanation: First conditional covers realistic future possibilities; second conditional covers imagined or unlikely present situations and polite proposals.
keyPoints: First: If I finish the course, I will ask for a promotion.
Second: If I had more time, I would study design.
Use were with I/he/she in formal second conditionals: If I were you...
grammar.example: If I pass the exam in June, I'll apply for the master's; if I had the money now, I'd already be enrolled.

items.prompt: If I ___ the exam in June, I will apply for the master's.
items.explanation: The first conditional uses the present simple in the if-clause.

items.prompt: If I had more time, I ___ a second language.
items.explanation: Imagined present situations take would + infinitive.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most diplomatic way to give advice?
options: If I am you, I apply.
If I were you, I would negotiate the salary.
If I was you, I will negotiate.
items.answer: If I were you, I would negotiate the salary.
items.explanation: 'If I were you, I would...' is the standard diplomatic formula.

inputs.title: Two planners, two routes
inputs.body: Host: Welcome back to Next Step. Today we are comparing two very different ways people plan the next twelve months. Tessa trained in graphic design at night while keeping her daytime office role, whereas Owen saved for a year and took a six-month break to retrain. Tessa, did having a fixed schedule help? Tessa: Definitely. I booked my evening studio sessions every Tuesday before work even started, so I knew I was going to finish my portfolio by June. If I had waited for spare energy at weekends, nothing would have happened. Host: And Owen, what convinced you to leave your job temporarily? Owen: Honestly, my workload was exhausting. If you work fifty hours a week, you rarely have headspace for creative study. I told myself that if I saved enough to cover rent, I would take the leap in October. I am starting an internship next Monday, and looking back, setting one clear deadline made every smaller choice much easier.

questions.prompt: How did Tessa make sure she finished her portfolio by June?
options: She resigned from her office job immediately
She booked regular Tuesday evening studio sessions in advance
She waited for free weekends to study
questions.answer: She booked regular Tuesday evening studio sessions in advance

questions.prompt: Why did Owen decide to take a six-month break?
options: His heavy workload left too little headspace for study
He wanted to move to another country permanently
questions.answer: His heavy workload left too little headspace for study

inputs.title: Why small milestones beat vague resolutions
inputs.body: Every January, millions of people announce ambitious plans to learn a language, change careers, or run a half-marathon. Yet by March, most of those promises quietly fade. Research on adult learning suggests the problem is rarely a lack of motivation; more often, the goal itself is too abstract to guide Tuesday evening decisions. Saying "I am going to improve my English" leaves too much room for hesitation, whereas committing to a fifteen-minute daily routine removes guesswork. When learners define concrete checkpoints—such as recording a ninety-second summary every Friday—progress becomes visible. Equally important is planning for realistic obstacles. If a busy week interrupts your usual timetable, having a backup slot protects momentum rather than triggering guilt. Goals succeed when they fit ordinary life, not only ideal weeks. For example, a trainee accountant studying part-time might block out Tuesday and Thursday mornings at seven-thirty before clients start calling. If an urgent audit disrupts Thursday, she already knows Sunday afternoon serves as her catch-up slot. Over sixteen weeks, those steady, realistic habits compound far more reliably than an exhausting burst of weekend cramming that ends before spring.

questions.prompt: According to the article, why do many resolutions fail by March?
options: Learners lack any motivation from the beginning
Goals are often too vague to guide daily choices
Fifteen-minute sessions are too short to matter
questions.answer: Goals are often too vague to guide daily choices

questions.prompt: What helps protect momentum during a busy week?
options: Waiting until next month to restart
Having a practical backup slot in your schedule
questions.answer: Having a practical backup slot in your schedule

modules.title: Daily life and social interaction
modules.summary: Express obligation, advice, ability, and polite permission naturally, and keep conversations flowing with clear questions and linkers.

grammar.name: Modals of obligation, advice, ability, permission
grammar.explanation: Choose between must / have to (strong obligation), should / ought to (advice), can / be able to (ability), and may / could (polite permission) according to social register.
keyPoints: Mustn’t expresses prohibition, whereas don’t have to means something is unnecessary.
Use could you / would you mind + -ing for polite everyday requests.
Use managed to or was able to (not could) for succeeding on one specific past occasion.
grammar.example: You don’t have to bring food to the flatwarming, though you ought to let Sam know if you are running late.

items.prompt: Entry to the community library is free, so visitors ___ pay a membership fee.
items.explanation: Lack of necessity takes "don’t have to", whereas "mustn’t" means forbidden.

items.prompt: Even though the train was delayed, Nadia ___ arrive before the meeting began.
items.explanation: Single-occasion past achievement uses "was able to" or "managed to", not "could".

items.prompt: ___ I borrow your umbrella until tomorrow morning?
items.explanation: "Could I..." is a natural, polite way to ask permission.

grammar.name: Question forms; basic linkers
grammar.explanation: Build accurate subject questions, indirect questions (Could you tell me where…?), and smooth everyday linkers (although, because, so, however).
keyPoints: Indirect questions keep statement word order: Do you know what time the café closes?
Subject questions need no auxiliary do/does: Who organised the street dinner?

inputs.title: Flatshare rules without the drama
inputs.body: Liam: Hey Chloe, could we have a quick word about the kitchen rota before everyone heads out? Chloe: Of course. Is everything alright? Liam: Yeah, mostly great, though we ought to agree on a simple rule for late-night washing-up. Nobody has to clean every pan straight after dinner if they are exhausted, so long as it is cleared before nine the next morning. Chloe: That sounds fair. Also, could you remind Sam that guests shouldn’t leave bikes in the narrow hallway? Last Tuesday I could barely open the front door with my shopping. Liam: Good point—I will mention it gently tonight. Do you know if everyone is free on Sunday afternoon to catch up over tea? Having a relaxed chat once a month stops small annoyances turning into big arguments.

questions.prompt: What does Liam suggest about washing-up after dinner?
options: Everyone must wash pans immediately at night
Dirty dishes should be cleared by nine the next morning
Only weekend guests should use the kitchen
questions.answer: Dirty dishes should be cleared by nine the next morning

questions.answer: Bikes had been left in the narrow hallway

inputs.title: The unwritten rules of good conversation
inputs.body: Many intermediate learners assume that good conversation in English depends on knowing rare idioms or speaking very quickly. In practice, people remember how easy you were to talk to, not how complicated your grammar sounded. One simple habit makes an immediate difference: asking open follow-up questions instead of firing rapid yes-or-no queries. For instance, asking "What made you choose that neighbourhood?" invites a story, whereas "Do you like your area?" often ends in a single word. Polite modal phrases also soften everyday requests. Saying "Would you mind lowering the volume a little?" keeps goodwill intact in shared offices or flats, whereas direct imperatives can sound unintentionally abrupt. Finally, small talk is rarely wasted effort. A two-minute chat about a local café or weekend plans signals warmth and builds trust before any serious discussion begins. Equally helpful is noticing turn-taking cues in lively groups. Pauses, brief summaries like "So you mean…", and friendly eye contact make quieter speakers feel welcome to contribute. When someone shares a different viewpoint, acknowledging what makes sense in their comment before adding your own keeps the atmosphere constructive rather than defensive—turns everyday small talk into genuine connection.

questions.prompt: Why does the text recommend open follow-up questions?
options: They invite stories rather than one-word answers
questions.answer: They invite stories rather than one-word answers

questions.prompt: How do polite modal phrases help in shared spaces?
options: They soften requests and protect goodwill
They replace the need to listen
questions.answer: They soften requests and protect goodwill

modules.title: Travel and cultural experiences
modules.summary: Describe heritage sites and travel logistics with the passive voice, and add vivid detail using relative clauses and comparatives.

grammar.name: Passive voice in present and past
grammar.explanation: Use the passive when the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is obvious, unknown or already understood.
keyPoints: Present passive: The old town is visited by two million people a year.
Past passive: The temple was built in the eleventh century.
Keep the agent with by only when it adds information.
grammar.example: The festival is celebrated every spring, and the square was decorated by local families for generations.

items.prompt: The temple ___ in the eleventh century.
items.explanation: A finished past action with an unknown or unimportant agent takes the past passive.

items.prompt: Choose the best sentence for a travel guide.
options: Two million people visit the old town every year.
The old town is visited by two million people every year.
The old town visits two million people every year.
items.answer: The old town is visited by two million people every year.
items.explanation: Guides foreground the place, so the passive keeps the old town as the topic.

items.prompt: When can 'by + agent' be dropped?
options: When the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant
items.answer: When the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant
items.explanation: The agent is optional; include it only if it carries new information.

grammar.name: Relative clauses; comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation: Defining clauses identify which person or place you mean and take no commas; non-defining clauses add extra information and always take commas.
keyPoints: Defining: The village that we visited is now a tourist trap.
Non-defining: Lisbon, which I visited last year, is crowded in August.
Never use that in a non-defining clause, and never drop the relative pronoun after a comma.
grammar.example: The guide, who grew up in the old quarter, showed us a market that no tourist ever finds.

items.prompt: Lisbon, ___ I visited last year, is crowded in August.
items.explanation: Non-defining clauses about a thing take which, never that.

items.prompt: Which sentence needs commas?
options: The guide who grew up here knows every street.
My brother who lives in Berlin is visiting.
items.explanation: Commas change meaning: with them the clause is extra information; without them it identifies the person.

items.prompt: The town ___ we stayed had no tourists at all.
items.explanation: Where replaces a place adverbial: we stayed in the town.

inputs.title: Travel podcast: the case for slow travel
inputs.body: People often ask me how many countries I have been to, and I have started saying that I have no idea, because the number tells you nothing. I spent three weeks in one town in Portugal last spring. I learned the baker's name. I was invited to a birthday party. That would never have happened if I had been moving every two days. Slow travel is not about seeing less; it is about being seen, and remembered, as a guest rather than a customer. Later in the episode, Elena compared two coastal towns she visited last autumn. In the first resort, dozens of identical souvenir shops had been built along the seafront, making the harbour far noisier than it used to be. In the second village, local guesthouses were run by families who cooked regional dishes and limited coach groups to small numbers. Staying four nights in one place, she argued, felt far more rewarding than rushing through four cities in four days.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject the country count?
options: It says nothing about the experience
It is too difficult to count
questions.answer: It says nothing about the experience

questions.prompt: What did she do last spring?
options: Stayed three weeks in one town
questions.answer: Stayed three weeks in one town

inputs.title: When tourism becomes too much
inputs.body: Venice is not alone. From Barcelona to Kyoto, cities that were built for residents are now shaped by visitors. Short-let flats have pushed rents up, and the bakery that survived for sixty years has been replaced by a shop selling souvenirs made elsewhere. Some cities have responded with visitor taxes, caps on cruise ships or bans on new short-term lets. None of these measures is popular with everyone. Yet the question behind them is simple: is a city a place to live, or a place to be seen? Most residents would answer both, and they would add that the balance has tipped. Residents in several historic centres say the real challenge is balancing hospitality with everyday life. When bakeries and hardware stores are replaced by short-term rentals, neighbourhoods lose the people who keep traditions alive. Yet solutions are possible when cities act early. Timed entry tickets, quieter pedestrian zones, and clear guidance on local customs help visitors feel welcome while protecting fragile streets. Travel works best when guests treat a destination as someone else’s home rather than a backdrop for photos.

questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
options: The effects of mass tourism on cities
The best time to visit Venice
questions.answer: The effects of mass tourism on cities
